title: Lewis Acid Site-Promoted Single-Atomic Cu Catalyzes Electrochemical CO2 Methanation
abstract: Developing an efficient catalyst for the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) is highly desired because of environmental and energy issues. Herein, we report a single-atomic-site Cu catalyst supported by a Lewis acid for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to CH4. Theoretical calculations suggested that Lewis acid sites in metal oxides (e.g., Al2O3, Cr2O3) can regulate the electronic structure of Cu atoms by optimizing intermediate absorption to promote CO2 methanation. Based on these theoretical results, ultrathin porous Al2O3 with enriched Lewis acid sites was explored as an anchor for Cu single atoms; this modification achieved a faradaic efficiency (FE) of 62% at −1.2 V (vs RHE) with a corresponding current density of 153.0 mA cm−2 for CH4 formation. This work demonstrates an effective strategy for tailoring the electronic structure of Cu single atoms for the highly efficient reduction of CO2 into CH4.

KEYWORDS: CO2RR, Lewis acid, Al2O3, single-atom Cu catalyst, CH4
The massive consumption of fossil energy has causedconsiderable carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions, which results in substantial climate change and global warming.1−3
The electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) is a promising way to convert CO2 into chemical fuels, effectively neutralizing CO2 emissions and ending the carbon cycle. 4−8 Moreover, this method could store intermittent renewable energy in the form of chemical bonds.9−11 However, the injection of electrons into CO2 for conversion to a product requires a highly negative potential and is often accompanied by poor activity as well as selectivity, which limits the commercialization of CO2 conversion.
12−14 Recently, singleatom catalysts (SAC) have exhibited well-defined and unique active centers and have achieved excellent activity and selectivity in the fields of electrocatalytic reactions, organic conversion, and environmental catalysis involving multiple pathways.15−22 In particular, Cu single-atom (SA) materials have shown promise for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. 23−26 As one important reduction product, CH4 is an important raw material for the manufacture of syngas and many other chemical products. It has good compatibility with existing chemical equipment and is promising for the substitution of fossil fuels.27 However, the performance of Cu SA materials in methane production still has certain limitations. It is highly desirable to develop representative Cu SACs for CO2 methanation with the aim of fundamentally solving these problems from theory to practice.
Lewis acids, such as some coordinated unsaturated metal atom sites (M), have been confirmed in recent years to be able to activate CO2 molecules and promote the production of methane.28−31 Among them, M centers can interact with the O in CO2 via Lewis acid−base interactions, which facilitate the cleavage of C−O bonds, thereby improving the catalytic activity.32−36 In addition, the high local acid concentration caused by the proton donor could make the acidic groups attach to the catalyst, and CO2 hydrogenation is, therefore, strongly promoted.37−40 As a typical Lewis acid support, alumina oxide (Al2O3) has been widely used in traditional catalysts because of its many advantages, such as earth abundance, high hardness, high melting point, good mechanical strength, corrosion and oxidation resistance.41−43 More importantly, its unique characteristics of a high reduction potential, abundant surface defects and hydrophilic surface that disperses metals well make it an ideal candidate for supporting and stabilizing SACs. However, it has received little attention in the electrocatalytic CO2RR, possibly because of its insulating properties.

Herein, we indeed find that loading Cu SA onto commercial Al2O3 and Cr2O3 Lewis acids
44 can significantly improve the activity of CO2 methanation, and the samples with stronger Lewis acidity perform better. Moreover, when Cu SAs are supported by ultrathin, porous Al2O3, the resulting catalyst exhibits a high selectivity of 62% toward CH4 with a corresponding current density of 153.0 mA cm−2 at −1.2 V (vs RHE). To clarify the effect of the Lewis acid sites on the Cu SA in catalyzing the CO2RR activity, we conducted density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Figure 1a, b show the
corresponding potential energy surfaces of the CO2RR (Figures S1−S3 and Table S1). For the Cu/Al2O3 SAC, the free energy change of the CO2 reduction to HCOO* was −0.25 eV, indicating that this step of (e− + H+) is thermodynamically favorable. The lower formation barrier of HCOO* than COOH* also reveals that the CH4 and CH3OH pathways preferentially proceed rather than the CO and HCOOH pathways. The proton−electron transfer of intermediate CH3O* then preferentially produces CH4 over CH3OH because the free energy increase of CH3O* → CH4O*(+0.21 eV) for CH4 is lower than the competitive CH3OH formation (+0.85 eV). Therefore, Cu/Al2O3 SAC is
beneficial for promoting CH4 production. However, when Cu SA is supported on the weak Lewis acid Cr2O3, the initial CO2* reaction pathways to HCOO* (+1.22 eV) and COOH* (+1.44 eV) are strongly endergonic, and the free energy change of this pathway is much higher than that of its counterpart. Therefore, the initial CO2RR activity of the Cr/ Cr2O3 SAC is poor. Hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) activity calculations reveal that Cu/Cr2O3 SAC is much more favorable to the HER than Cu/Al2O3 SAC (Figure S4). The binding energy of Cu atoms on Al2O3(311) surface is −4.79 eV, and the cohesive energy of Cu bulk is −4.09 eV, suggesting that the supported Cu SAs are sufficiently stable against sintering. Bader charge analysis shows that the Cu atom on Al2O3 is in a higher oxidation state than that on Cr2O3 (electron transfer occurs from the Cu atom to the support). In addition, the Cu atom on Al2O3 shows a higher d-band center than that on Cr2O3 (−1.58 vs −1.95 eV), suggesting an improved electron transfer capability in electrocatalytic reactions (Figure 1c, d). The lower electron accumulation on the Cu SA sites is favorable for combining with electron-rich groups during the CO2RR. Therefore, the electron-accepting characteristics of Lewis acid sites are beneficial for stabilizing the CO2 methanation intermediate and reducing the overall reaction energy barrier. Theoretical calculations show that the surface electrons of Cu SA are attracted to Lewis acid sites, forming a favorable reaction pathway for methane generation. To confirm the theoretical prediction, Lewis acid (e.g., commercial Al2O3 and Cr2O3, denoted as C−Al2O3 and C− Cr2O3 here after, Figure S5) supported Cu SA were prepared to catalyze the CO2 methanation. From X-ray diffraction (XRD) in Figure S6a, no Cu metal signal peaks are observed, preliminarily confirming the formation of Al2O3 or Cr2O3 supported Cu SA (abbreviated as Cu/C−Al2O3 SACs and Cu/ C−Cr2O3 SACs). The temperature-programmed ammonia desorption (NH3-TPD) result confirms that the Cu/C−Al2O3 SAC exhibits a stronger Lewis acidity than the Cu/C−Cr2O3 SAC (Figure 2a). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) shows that the Cu 2p level of the Cu/C−Al2O3 SAC is +0.6 eV more positive than that of the Cu/C−Cr2O3 SAC (Figure S6b), which indicates that the Cu around Al has a less positive charge; this observation is consistent with the theoretical results. The CO2RR performances of the Cu/C−Al2O3 and Cu/C− Cr2O3 SACs were evaluated (Figures S7 and S8). 45 The linear sweep voltammetry curves (LSV) show that the Cu/C−Al2O3 SAC exhibits a higher current density response than the Cu/ C−Cr2O3 SAC, suggesting that the stronger Lewis acid has higher activity for the CO2RR (Figure 2b). Figure 2c, d shows the faradaic efficiencies (FEs) of all products obtained during the CO2RR. The products of the Cu/C−Al2O3 SAC reaction are mainly CH4 (the maximum FE reached 38%), ethanol and CO with a small amount of H2 (below 25%). In contrast, the Cu/C−Cr2O3 SAC displays a weaker CO2RR activity. The products are mainly H2 (FE > 60%) with a small amount of CH4 (FE < 10%). Therefore, there is a certain correlation between the Lewis acidity of the catalyst and its CO2RR activity (mainly CH4). The FE for CH4 increases with the Lewis acidity: Cu/C−Cr2O3 SAC < Cu/C−Al2O3 SAC. This comparison highlights the key role of the Lewis acid site in promoting the reduction of CO2 to CH4. This result is consistent with the theoretical prediction that the presence of Lewis acid sites could act to tailor the electronic structure of

the resident copper atom and stabilize the CO2RR intermediates. Therefore, it is reasonable to expect the enhanced
performance of Cu SACs when ultrathin porous nanostructures are employed because these nanostructures can provide abundant Lewis acid sites and benefit the electrons transportation.46,47 An ultrathin porous Al2O3 nanosheet was successfully prepared by a hydrothermal method, and the Cu SA was then loaded onto it with the same method described above (the product was abbreviated as Cu/p-Al2O3 SAC, Figure S9). The TEM image shows that the Cu/p-Al2O3 SAC exhibits an ultrathin porous sheetlike morphology (Figure 3a). The XRD pattern of the Cu/p-Al2O3 SAC is consistent with that of the standard orthorhombic crystal Al2O3 (PDF #29− 0063) and does not show the characteristic peak of Cu particles, which preliminarily shows that Cu is trapped in a single atom state (Figure S10a). High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) shows an interplanar spacing of 0.23 nm, corresponding to the (311) plane of the p-Al2O3 (Figure 3b). The elemental mapping results demonstrate that O, Al and Cu are evenly dispersed over the entire architecture (Figure 3c). The mass loading of Cu in the Cu/p-Al2O3 SAC is 1.8 wt %, as determined by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) (Figure S10b). The Cu 2p 3/2 peak in the XPS spectrum is located at 932.8, which is located between those of the Cu/C−Al2O3 SAC and the Cu/C−Cr2O3 SAC (Figure S11). Compared with that of Al2O3, the Al 2p peak in the Cu/ p-Al2O3 SAC is at a lower binding energy (0.15 eV), and the O 1s peak appears at a higher binding energy. These results indicate that the surface electrons of Cu are transferred to Al2O3,
48 resulting in a much greater preference for binding electron-rich intermediate species in the methanation process.49,50
Aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC HAADF-STEM) clearly shows that several bright dots representing individual Cu atoms appear on the nanosheet (Figure 3d). X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) measurements were further conducted to study the local atomic and electronic structural information on Cu SA species on p-Al2O3. The X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectrum shows that the white line of the Cu/p-Al2O3 SAC is relatively close to that of CuO, indicating that the valence state of the Cu SA is close to +2 (Figure 3e).51,52 The extended X-ray absorption fine structure spectrum (EXAFS) reveals that the Cu−O contribution of approximately 1.5 Å is the only prominent shell in the Cu/pAl2O3 SAC. In addition, the contribution of the scattering peak of Cu−Cu coordination is not observed in the 2 to 4 Å region, further suggesting that only atomically dispersed Cu catalysts are present in the Cu/p-Al2O3 SAC (Figure 3f). The fitting results show that the Cu−O coordination number in the Cu/pAl2O3 SAC is 3.31 ± 0.30 (Figure S12 and Table S2). The CO2RR performance of the Cu/p-Al2O3 SAC was also determined (Figure 4, Figures S13−15). As shown in the LSV, the Cu/p-Al2O3 SAC displays a larger CO2 response current density than the Al2O3 and the Cu/C−Al2O3 SAC (Figure 4a, Figure 2d). Figure 4b shows that the Cu/p-Al2O3 SAC has excellent CH4 selectivity with a maximum FE of 62% at −1.2 V and a partial current density of 94.8 mA cm−2. The ultrathin porous nanosheet structure of Cu/p-Al2O3 SAC remained unchanged after CO2RR, indicating its considerable stability (Figure S16). Compared to that of the Cu/C−Al2O3 SAC, the enhanced CH4 FE over the Lewis acid site-enriched Cu/pAl2O3 SAC further implies the critical role of Lewis acid sites in CH4 formation. The lack of CH4 detected demonstrates that CO2 methanation is not due to the role of the p-Al2O3 support

(Figure 4c). In addition, a pyridine poisoning test was used to further prove that Lewis acidity is essential for CH4 formation.44,53,54 Once the Lewis acid sites (octahedral Al− O) were effectively poisoned by pyridine (1% in 1.0 M KOH), the CO2RR performance was significantly reduced, and the CH4 selectivity was decreased to ∼15% over the entire potential range (Figure 4d). To illustrate the promoting effect of Lewis acids on SAs, Cu nanoparticles (NPs) supported on ultrathin p-Al2O3 (denoted Cu NPs/p-Al2O3; Figure S17) were prepared. Cu NPs/p-Al2O3 showed a lower current density than the Cu/p-Al2O3 SAC and lower CH4 selectivity (FEmax < 40%, Figure 4e). The Cu/p-Al2O3 SAC displays a higher turnover frequency (TOF = 5620 h−1) for CH4 than the Cu NPs/p-Al2O3 SAC (Figure 4f). Therefore, Lewis acids could regulate Cu SA species. This series of tests has confirmed the excellent CO2 methanation activity of Cu/Al2O3 SAC (Table S3).
■ CONCLUSIONS In this work, we theoretically and experimentally show the crucial role of the Lewis acid in a Cu/Al2O3 SAC for electrochemical CO2 reduction to CH4. Specifically, an ultrathin p-Al2O3-supported Cu SAC was developed. This catalyst has an FE of CH4 approaching 62% at −1.2 V vs RHE, and the corresponding current density reaches 153.0 mA cm−2. Our results demonstrate that CO2 hydrogenation to methane is promoted on Lewis acid oxide-supported Cu SA. This work provides a blueprint for predicting and describing the promotion of metal oxides, which is ubiquitous in heterogeneous single-atom catalysis.
